title: Days, dates, and making plans
title_target: ນັດພົບກັນ — Nat phop kan
goal: Say days and dates, make and change plans, and turn down invitations without offending anyone — a social skill that matters more in Laos than grammar.

dialogs.title: ບົດສົນທະນາ — Setting a time for dinner together
dialogs.intro: Bounmy invites Budi to dinner. Notice how long they negotiate the time before agreeing — and that nobody ever says "no" directly.

lines.speaker: ບຸນມີ:
lines.text: [ບູດີ|Buu-dii] [ຄືນ|khʉ́ʉn][ວັນ|wán][ສຸກ|súk][ຫວ່າງ|wàang][ບໍ່|bàw]
lines.id: Budi, are you free Friday evening?

lines.speaker: ບູດີ:
lines.text: [ວັນ|Wán][ສຸກ|súk][ບໍ່|bàw][ຄ່ອຍ|khàwy][ສະດວກ|sa-dùak] [ມີ|Míi][ວຽກ|wîak][ຢູ່|yùu]
lines.id: Friday's not great. I have work.
lines.literal: day — Friday — not — very — convenient. have — work — (ongoing).

lines.speaker: ບຸນມີ:
lines.text: [ຄັນ|Khán][ຊັ້ນ|sân] [ວັນ|wán][ເສົາ|sǎo][ເດ|dee] [ໄປ|Pai][ກິນ|kin][ເຂົ້າ|khào][ແລງ|léeng][ນຳ|nám][ກັນ|kan][ດີ|dii][ບໍ່|bàw]
lines.id: Then how about Saturday? Shall we have dinner together?
lines.literal: if — so — day — Saturday — how-about? go — eat — rice — evening — along — together — good — (question)?

lines.speaker: ບູດີ:
lines.text: [ດີ|Dii][ເລີຍ|lóei] [ຈັກ|Ják][ໂມງ|móong][ດີ|dii]

lines.speaker: ບຸນມີ:
lines.text: [ຫົກ|Hók][ໂມງ|móong][ແລງ|léeng][ໄດ້|dâi][ບໍ່|bàw] [ຮ້ານ|Hâan][ຢູ່|yùu][ແຄມ|kheem][ຂອງ|Khǒong]
lines.id: Is six in the evening okay? The place is on the Mekong riverbank.
lines.literal: six — o'clock — evening — can — (question)? restaurant — at — bank — Khong.

lines.speaker: ບູດີ:
lines.text: [ໄດ້|Dâi] [ແຕ່|Tèe][ຂໍ|khǎw][ເລື່ອນ|lʉ̂an][ເປັນ|pen][ຫົກ|hók][ໂມງ|móong][ເຄິ່ງ|khòeng][ໄດ້|dâi][ບໍ່|bàw] [ຂ້ອຍ|Khàwy][ເລີກ|lôek][ວຽກ|wîak][ຊ້າ|sâa]
lines.id: Okay. But could we push it to half past six? I finish work late.
lines.literal: can. but — ask — move — become — six — o'clock — half — can — (question)? I — stop — work — late.

lines.speaker: ບຸນມີ:
lines.text: [ໄດ້|Dâi][ເລີຍ|lóei] [ຫົກ|Hók][ໂມງ|móong][ເຄິ່ງ|khòeng][ເນາະ|nāw] [ຂ້ອຍ|Khàwy][ຊິ|si][ຈອງ|jawng][ໂຕະ|tó][ໄວ້|wâi]
lines.id: Sure. Half past six, then. I'll book a table.
lines.literal: can — right-away. six — o'clock — half — isn't-it? I — will — book — table — keep.

lines.speaker: ບູດີ:
lines.text: [ຂອບໃຈ|Khàwp-jai] [ວັນ|Wán][ທີ|thíi][ເທົ່າໃດ|thao-dai][ນໍ|náw]

lines.speaker: ບຸນມີ:
lines.text: [ວັນ|Wán][ທີ|thíi][ສິບ|síp][ຫ້າ|hāa] [ເດືອນ|Dʉan][ຫົກ|hók]
lines.literal: day — number — ten — five. month — six.

lines.speaker: ບູດີ:
lines.text: [ຈື່|Jʉ̀ʉ][ໄວ້|wâi][ແລ້ວ|lèeo] [ຖ້າ|Thàa][ຂ້ອຍ|khàwy][ມາ|maa][ຊ້າ|sâa] [ຂ້ອຍ|khàwy][ຊິ|si][ໂທ|thóo][ຫາ|hǎa][ເຈົ້າ|jâo]
lines.id: Got it written down. If I'm late, I'll call you.
lines.literal: remember — keep — already. if — I — come — late — I — will — phone — seek — you.

lines.speaker: ບຸນມີ:
lines.text: [ໄດ້|Dâi] [ພົບ|Phop][ກັນ|kan][ວັນ|wán][ເສົາ|sǎo][ເດີ້|dòe]

notes: **Day names always begin with ວັນ *wán* (day).** *ວັນຈັນ* (Monday), *ວັນສຸກ* (Friday). Don't drop *ວັນ* — without it, *ຈັນ* alone means "the moon."
**ຫວ່າງ wàang = "free, empty," ບໍ່ຫວ່າງ = busy.** Asking *ຫວ່າງບໍ່* is the most common way to open an invitation. Compare *ຫຍຸ້ງ nyûng*, which means busy in the sense of "lots going on."

**ບໍ່ຄ່ອຍສະດວກ bàw khàwy sa-dùak = "not very convenient," and this is how Lao people say no.** A flat *ບໍ່ໄດ້* (can't) sounds harsh to Lao ears. The gentle way is to mention an inconvenience, not a refusal — much like "hmm, that's a bit tricky" in English.
**ຄັນຊັ້ນ khán sân = "in that case."** It introduces the next suggestion after the first is turned down, and it comes up constantly in Lao conversation. Its shorter twin: *ຊັ້ນ sân*.
**…ດີບໍ່ dii bàw = "how about…?", …ໄດ້ບໍ່ dâi bàw = "can we…?"** The first asks for an opinion, the second asks whether it's possible. Both go at the end of the sentence, and both are very polite.

**ນຳກັນ nám kan = "together."** *ໄປກິນເຂົ້ານຳກັນ* = "let's go eat together." The word *ກັນ kan* alone means "each other, together," and it appears in many expressions: *ພົບກັນ* (meet), *ຮູ້ຈັກກັນ* (know each other), *ຄືກັນ* (the same).
**ໄວ້ wâi after a verb means "set aside for later."** *ຈອງໄວ້* (book ahead), *ຈື່ໄວ້* (remember well), *ເກັບໄວ້* (put away). It's a subtle marker that makes sentences sound much more natural.

**Dates are built as ວັນທີ + number, then ເດືອນ + month number.** *ວັນທີສິບຫ້າ ເດືອນຫົກ* = the 15th of month 6 (June). Official month names exist, but they're long and rarely spoken; giving the month number is always correct and always understood.
**ນໍ náw at the end of a sentence is a "hmm?" you ask yourself.** Unlike *ເນາະ nāw*, which invites agreement, *ນໍ* is more like thinking aloud: *ວັນທີເທົ່າໃດນໍ* (what's the date again?).

grammars.title: Seven days, and week markers
after: The pattern **ໜ້າ *nâa*** (front, next) and **ແລ້ວ *lèeo*** (past) works with every time unit: *ເດືອນໜ້າ* (next month), *ປີແລ້ວ* (last year), *ມື້ໜ້າ* (some other day). Learn those two words and the whole system opens up.

after: ⚠️ *ໄວ້ເທື່ອໜ້າເນາະ* (maybe next time) is the refusal you'll hear most and the one foreigners most often misread. It rarely means "next time" — usually it means "no, but I don't want to say so." Accept it with a smile and don't push.

blocks.text: Use the **in speech** column for talking and recognize the **official name** column for reading — official names appear on documents, tickets, and notice boards. Full date order: *ວັນເສົາ ວັນທີສິບຫ້າ ເດືອນຫົກ ປີສອງພັນຊາວຫ້າ* — weekday, date, month, year, from smallest to largest.

blocks.text: The word **ບຸນ *bun*** means both "festival" and "merit" — every Lao festival is rooted in the idea of building up good deeds. If you're invited to a *ບຸນ*, it's a sincere invitation and you should go; turning down a festival invitation is felt much more than turning down an ordinary dinner.

During *ບຸນປີໃໝ່ລາວ* in April, offices close for days and anyone on the street may get splashed with water — including you. Keeping your phone in a plastic bag is sensible preparation, and getting angry about being wet is the fastest way to ruin the mood.
